opus-5.5.text:
I think the contribution of ConvNeXt is a bit different from what people might expect from a typical "new architecture" paper. If you look at it purely technically, there's almost nothing truly new in it. Every component we used, like larger kernels, depthwise convolutions, the inverted bottleneck, LayerNorm, GELU, and fewer activation layers, already existed somewhere in the literature. So I never really saw it as inventing something.

What I think it contributed was more of a perspective, or maybe a correction to a narrative. Around 2020 and 2021, after Vision Transformers and especially Swin Transformer came out, there was a strong feeling in the community that convolutions were outdated, and that Transformers were simply better for vision because of attention, because they have less inductive bias, and so on. A lot of people were ready to move on from ConvNets entirely.

What we wanted to ask was a very simple question. How much of the improvement actually comes from attention itself, and how much comes from all the other things that changed at the same time, like the training recipe, the macro design, the normalization, the data augmentation? So we took a standard ResNet and modernized it step by step toward the design of a Transformer, without using any attention, and tracked how the accuracy changed. It turned out that a pure ConvNet could match or even outperform Swin on ImageNet, detection, and segmentation, with a quite clean design.

So I'd say the paper was partly an empirical study and partly a kind of "controlled experiment" for the field. The message wasn't that ConvNets are better than Transformers. It was that we should be careful about which design choices are really responsible for progress. Many of the gains people attributed to the Transformer architecture were actually coming from training techniques and system-level design decisions.

Looking back, I also think it had a practical impact. ConvNeXt became a strong, simple baseline that people in industry and in downstream tasks could use, because convolutions are still very efficient and easy to deploy. And it helped people think of architecture design as less tribal. It's not ConvNet versus Transformer as two religions. These are design spaces that can borrow from each other.

Of course, I should be honest that the broader trend has gone toward Transformers, especially with scaling, multimodal models, and unified architectures across language and vision. So ConvNeXt didn't "save" ConvNets in the long run, and that was never really the goal. For me its value is more in the methodology: question the narrative, run careful ablations, and understand where the gains actually come from. I think that mindset is still important today, maybe even more so, now that so many things are changing at once in large-scale models.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think ConvNeXt's contribution is more about asking a question than inventing something new. Around 2021 the whole field had kind of decided that Transformers had won, that attention was fundamentally better, and convolution was yesterday's idea. And I remember thinking, wait, is that actually true? Or is it that Swin Transformer and ViT came with a whole new generation of training recipes, data augmentation, AdamW, longer schedules, and ConvNets were still being compared using the 2015 ResNet setup?

So the paper is really an experiment in controlling for that. We took a standard ResNet-50 and, step by step, modernized it. Change the training recipe, change the stage ratio, use a patchify stem, go to depthwise convolution with large kernels, inverted bottleneck, swap BatchNorm for LayerNorm, GELU instead of ReLU, fewer activations and normalization layers. Each step is a tiny thing, almost boring. But by the end you have a pure ConvNet that matches or beats Swin on ImageNet, COCO, ADE20K, and it scales just as well.

What I'm most proud of is not the number. It's that it changed the conversation. It made people realize a lot of the gains attributed to attention were actually gains from the overall design and training philosophy, and that architecture comparisons need to be done carefully. The paper is written almost like a story, with that one roadmap figure, and I think that's why it got adopted, people could follow the reasoning and reuse the pieces.

The honest limitation is that it's a paper about the vision backbone in isolation. Transformers have real advantages when you go multimodal, when you want one architecture for text, images, and everything else. ConvNeXt doesn't address that, and I wouldn't claim it does. So I'd say it was the right paper at the right time, a kind of reality check, and I'm happy it's still used as a strong, simple baseline. But I don't think of it as a final answer about convolution versus attention. If anything, the lesson is that the dichotomy was never the important part.

astra-6.text:
I think the main contribution was to make the comparison between ConvNets and Transformers more controlled. When a new architecture performs better, it’s easy to attribute the improvement to its defining component—in this case, self-attention. But training recipes and many other architectural choices are changing at the same time. How much of the improvement actually comes from attention?

With ConvNeXt, we started with a conventional ConvNet and modernized it step by step, borrowing design choices from hierarchical vision Transformers. The result showed that a pure ConvNet could still be very competitive. That gave us a reason to reconsider the idea that convolution itself had become the bottleneck.

I wouldn’t interpret that as saying ConvNets are universally better than Transformers. To me, the more useful contribution is methodological: before we declare one architecture superior, we should give the baseline the same care. Otherwise, we may mistake a better-designed system for evidence that one particular component is essential.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the main contribution was to challenge an assumption: that the improvements we were seeing from vision Transformers necessarily came from the attention mechanism itself. Architecture, training recipes, and many other choices had changed at the same time, so it was difficult to separate their effects.

With ConvNeXt, we asked how far a conventional ConvNet could go if we modernized it systematically, borrowing useful design choices from Transformers while keeping it fully convolutional. The result suggested that convolution was still a very competitive building block.

To me, the value is less about declaring a winner between ConvNets and Transformers and more about making the comparison clearer. When a new model performs better, which changes actually explain the improvement? ConvNeXt offered a strong baseline for asking that question.
